title: Pulse Engineering of Quantum Many-Body Dynamics: Emergent Scar States, Entanglement, and Nonstabilizerness
authors: Prasant Mallik, Arkaprava Sil, Sudipto Singha Roy
abstract: Understanding and coherently controlling the properties of interacting quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in non-equilibrium quantum physics. While in the past decades, a wide range of many-body Hamiltonians have been introduced to study quantum chaos, atypical eigenstates, and quantum resources, systematically engineering and continuously tuning these properties within a single microscopic model remains largely unexplored. Here, we employ a pulse engineering scheme to construct an effective Hamiltonian that continuously interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg (XXX) chain with a local impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian. Along this interpolation, we identify several families of analytically tractable atypical eigenstates embedded in the excited-state spectrum with distinct entanglement and nonstabilizerness properties. In the XXX limit, these states exhibit exact plateaus in both entanglement and stabilizer Rényi entropy and correspond to coherent superpositions of long-range valence-bond solid (VBS) states. As the pulse strength increases, the effective Hamiltonians exhibit a hierarchy of new set of approximate entanglement plateaus in the low-energy spectrum. Interestingly, in the fully pulse-engineered ZX limit, we uncover a distinct pair of long-range entangled stabilizer eigenstates, corresponding to rainbow scar states. We further show that pulse engineering preserves the distinct chaotic and non-chaotic regimes of the original model, while that is largely absent in the dynamical generation of entanglement and nonstabilizerness. The pulse-engineered models generate nearly identical quantum resources in both regimes, revealing a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum-resource generation. Our results establish pulse engineering as a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources.
summary: The paper introduces pulse engineering as a powerful technique to construct and study effective Hamiltonians for interacting spin chains. By smoothly interpolating between two distinct models (XXX and ZX), the authors demonstrate controlled access to exotic eigenstates exhibiting specific entanglement patterns. This establishes pulse engineering as a general tool for tuning quantum resources in many-body physics.
main_problem: The central challenge is coherently controlling the properties of interacting quantum many-body systems by systematically engineering their Hamiltonians.
main_result: Pulse engineering provides a versatile framework to generate structured Hamiltonians, allowing for controlled transitions between different types of atypical eigenstates (like VBS states and rainbow scar states) while tracking changes in entanglement and nonstabilizerness.
method: The authors use pulse engineering schemes combined with average Hamiltonian theory to derive an effective time-independent Hamiltonian that interpolates between two known models ($\mathcal{H}_{XXX}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{ZX}$).
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional spin-1/2 chain with nearest-neighbor interactions and a local impurity. The analysis compares the chaotic Heisenberg (XXX) model to a target ZX Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Entanglement entropy, stabilizer Rényi entropy, nonstabilizerness ('magic'), and spectral statistics ($\langle r angle$).
important_parameters: The interpolation parameter $ eta$ controls the mixing between the two Hamiltonians; regimes include exchange-dominated ($J/\epsilon > 1$) and impurity-dominated ($J/\epsilon < 1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the leading-order Magnus approximation for deriving the effective Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the pulse-driven spin chain, the resulting effective Hamiltonian structure, and show how entanglement/nonstabilizerness evolve across different engineered limits.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of control in many-body systems, derives the effective Hamiltonian via pulse engineering theory, analyzes the system's spectral properties (chaos vs. non-chaos) across the parameter space, and finally characterizes specific atypical eigenstates and their associated quantum resources.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses how external driving fields can be used as a tool to sculpt complex many-body Hamiltonians, offering precise control over emergent quantum features like entanglement structure, which is highly relevant for designing quantum simulators.
